items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. items.t: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears. Cuando el reloj marque las 2:00 a. m. , los ciudadanos deberán atrasar los relojes una hora , por lo que la hora local volverá a ser la 1:00 a. m. El cambio de hora anual busca devolver la claridad a las primeras horas de la mañana, otorgando una hora adicional de descanso durante la madrugada. Aunque gran parte de los dispositivos inteligentes y teléfonos celulares se actualizan de manera automática, las autoridades recomiendan revisar relojes mecánicos y sistemas que no cuenten con conexión a Internet para evitar confusiones en los compromisos laborales y escolares del lunes siguiente. items.t: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century. This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. items.t: 2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history. With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms. “It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University. Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars. items.x: LAKE CHARLES, La. (KPLC) - The Lake Charles Charter Academy (LCCA) Chargers middle school football team beat Cecila 42-6 in the state tournament at the Caesars Superdome this past weekend. Sixth-grade quarterback Mark Honore and receivers Jericho and Jeziel Livings are names to watch on Friday nights in the coming years.

items.t: 71-year-old grandmother missing after going on walk more than 3 weeks ago, police say
items.x: (Gray News) - A 71-year-old New Jersey woman went for a walk more than three weeks ago and hasn’t been seen since. Belinda Prentice was last seen about 6 p.m. Oct. 5 near Bamburgh Court off New Brunswick Road and Willow Avenue in Franklin Township, a press release said. Her granddaughter, Sienna Benjamin, said Prentice had shown signs of cognitive decline in recent years, and the family was working to determine whether she had dementia and to obtain guardianship, People reported. Franklin Township police and the family are urging residents to check doorbell and security cameras for possible sightings. Anyone with information is asked to call the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-2300.

items.t: 79-year-old man killed after collision with fire truck
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. ( KWCH /Gray News) - A 79-year-old man was killed in a crash involving a fire truck. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

Pike fue sentenciada a muerte por el asesinato de Collen Slemmer en 1995. En septiembre, sobrevivió a dos dosis del medicamento utilizado para la inyección letal. Después del intento fallido, Pike pasó varios días hospitalizada y regresó a prisión. Actualmente puede hablar en oraciones completas y caminar por sí misma. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: Trump slams Peltola campaign over two Sullivans on Alaska ballot
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump and Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are accusing Democrats of intentionally trying to confuse Alaska voters, after two candidates named Dan Sullivan appeared on the state’s midterm election ballot for U.S. Senate. Trump is among several Republicans criticizing Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, accusing her of perpetuating a fraud on Alaska voters. The New York Times reported Wednesday that campaign staffers for Peltola, a former Alaska congresswoman now running for the U.S. Senate, tried to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The effort is not illegal. However, the reports have led Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, to order an investigation into alleged election manipulation. Trump commented on the controversy Thursday before leaving for South Carolina. “So nobody’s going to know what to do.

items.t: Baby dies after 15-year-old girl gives birth at elementary school, reports say
items.x: CHICAGO — Authorities are reportedly investigating the death of a baby after a teen girl gave birth at an elementary school in the Chicago area on Wednesday. Chicago police shared that a 15-year-old girl gave birth at Aldridge Elementary School on East 131st Street, but the baby was pronounced dead at the scene. WLS reports that the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office listed the location of the death as 630 E. 131st St. in Chicago, which is the address for Aldridge Elementary School. The teen girl was reportedly in good condition when taken to an area hospital for treatment. Officials from the elementary school did not immediately comment on the situation, WGN reported.

items.t: 16-year-old killed in tractor crash with semi-truck, officials say
items.x: AUDUBON, Iowa ( KCRG /Gray News) - A teen is dead after being thrown from a tractor in a crash with a semi-truck. Iowa State Patrol said it happened Sunday night on Highway 71, just south of Audubon. A crash report said a semi-truck hit the back of the trailer that the tractor was pulling. Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene. The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries. Crash reports showed this was the second farm equipment crash that happened in Audubon County on Sunday. The other crash left a pickup truck driver with serious injuries after it crashed head-on with a combine.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.t: Space heaters under recall after units reportedly catch fire
items.x: (Gray News) - Almost 340,000 space heaters are under recall throughout the United States due to the risk of fire and burns. DREO space heaters model DR-HSH015 were placed under recall on Oct. 29, the Consumer Product Safety Commission reported. About 338,800 units were affected, with an additional 36,300 sold in Canada. They were sold directly through DREO and other sites like Best Buy and Home Depot between Sept. 2025 and Oct. 2026. According to the recall, the affected space heaters can overheat and catch fire. DREO said they received 17 reports of ignition, three resulting in property damage and one burning a person’s hand. Anyone with a recalled unit should stop using the space heater immediately and contact DREO for a free space heater to replace the faulty one. items.t: ‘Star Trek’ actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
items.x: (AP) - Patrick Stewart , the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises, has died. He was 86. Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed. While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of “A Christmas Carol” and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen. items.t: Lake Charles man who died in Harrison County, Texas trailer house fire identified
items.x: HARRISON COUNTY, Texas (KSLA) - A man died Saturday morning, Oct. 17, after a trailer house fire at a deer ranch on McCauley Road in Scottsville, Texas, according to the Harrison County Fire Department. The Justice of the Peace in Harrison County, Judge John D. Oswalt, has confirmed the identity of the man to be Dr. James C. Barrow , 47, of Lake Charles. Officials say a burn pit was left burning, and the flames spread outside the pit, catching the porch of the trailer house on fire. Three people were inside the home when the fire started. Two were able to escape, and one person died, officials say. A 47-year-old Lake Charles man died Saturday morning, Oct. 17 following a trailer house fire at a deer ranch on McCauley Road in Scottsville, Texas. Identities of the survivors have not yet been released.

items.x: LAREDO, Texas (Telemundo Gray News) — Un agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza de EE. UU. en Texas ha sido acusado en relación con la muerte de su esposa. Abel Garza, de 30 años, ha sido acusado de asesinato, un delito grave de primer grado, por la muerte de su esposa, Mayra Alejandra Landeros, de 28 años, tras un altercado doméstico en el sur de Laredo. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. items.t: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age

Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International , said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago. items.x: (Gray News) - Kyle Chrisley, son of reality television star Todd Chrisley, has pleaded guilty to resisting arrest in an incident from December 2025. Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. According to Us Magazine , the remaining charges were dismissed. He was arrested Dec. 20 after his wife called police, reportedly saying he was “belligerent.” When police arrived, Chrisley reportedly punched multiple officers . items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. Students in Susan Meunier’s new leadership class are tracing and painting portraits of pets. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. Start with the question the trial is trying to answer Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to change the question you ask. “I think the first thing we have to do is not think about, ‘Can this clinical trial help me?’ but ‘What is this clinical trial trying to answer?’” Rogers said. “That’s what most of these trials are about.” A trial is not a last resort Rogers said many people see clinical trials as a last resort. “I think a lot of people think that it’s a last resort option, that you don’t have anything else, when in fact one of th

items.t: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. items.t: How art therapy helps patients connect with caregivers
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears. items.x: TUSCALOOSA, Ala. ( WBRC ) - As Domestic Violence Awareness Month comes to a close, dozens of women gathered in Tuscaloosa to share stories of survival and support victims of abusive relationships during the eighth annual Purple Purse Luncheon. The annual event raises awareness and critical funding for Turning Point, a Tuscaloosa-area agency providing support services to individuals and families impacted by domestic violence. Attendees were not required to share personal experiences; organizers noted that simply being present in the room showed survivors they do not have to carry their struggles alone or feel ashamed. “Women from all walks of life are now coming forward,” organizer Michele Coley told WBRC. “Every year I get three or four inboxes on Facebook. ‘When are we having it? items.t: Who’s bankrolling Alabama’s governors race?
items.x: BIRMINGHAM, Ala. ( WBRC ) - Republican U.S. Sen. Tommy Tuberville has raised nearly $11 million more than Democrat Doug Jones in the race for Alabama governor, and the two campaigns are funded by very different mixes of donors, according to a 6 On Your Side Investigates analysis of campaign finance records. Ahead of the general election, WBRC reviewed the contributions and spending each campaign reported to the Alabama Secretary of State through Oct. 27, 2026. Tuberville’s campaign reported its first contributions on May 27, 2025, about six months before Jones entered the race on Nov. 24, 2025. Since then, Tuberville has raised about $17.7 million. Jones has raised more than $6.7 million. items.t: 2 airlifted to hospital after crash involving garbage truck in Hueytown
items.x: HUEYTOWN, Ala. ( WBRC ) - Two people were airlifted two a hospital after a crash in Hueytown Thursday, police said. According to Hueytown Police, a garbage truck and car were involved in a wreck on John’s Road near a water treatment facility. Police said four people were in the car and all suffered injuries. Officials said two of them were airlifted to a hospital with life-threatening injuries and the other two were taken to a hospital by ambulance. The driver of the garbage truck was not hurt, police said. John’s Road was initially closed due to the crash, but police said the road has since reopened. This time, the two men are vying to be Alabama’s 55th governor. Tuberville easily defeated Jones in the 2020 U.S. Senate race, receiving more than 60% of votes . Jones’ biggest vote margin in that race came in Jefferson County, where he beat Tuberville by about 56,000 votes. Six years later, Jefferson County is again Jones’ strongest base, this time providing nearly half of the itemized money he has raised in Alabama, according to a WBRC analysis of campaign finance records available as of Oct. 27. items.t: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century. This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. items.t: 2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history. With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms. “It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University. Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars. items.t: 71-year-old grandmother missing after going on walk more than 3 weeks ago, police say
items.x: (Gray News) - A 71-year-old New Jersey woman went for a walk more than three weeks ago and hasn’t been seen since. Belinda Prentice was last seen about 6 p.m. Oct. 5 near Bamburgh Court off New Brunswick Road and Willow Avenue in Franklin Township, a press release said. Her granddaughter, Sienna Benjamin, said Prentice had shown signs of cognitive decline in recent years, and the family was working to determine whether she had dementia and to obtain guardianship, People reported. Franklin Township police and the family are urging residents to check doorbell and security cameras for possible sightings. Anyone with information is asked to call the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-2300.

In fact, Rominger said she’s dealing with it now. “I’m already a water drinker, but the antihistamine I take makes me thirsty during the day, so I make sure I drink extra water during that,” said Rominger. Like all of us, Rominger has had her bouts with infections.

items.t: 79-year-old man killed after collision with fire truck
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. ( KWCH /Gray News) - A 79-year-old man was killed in a crash involving a fire truck. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

items.t: Child care costs squeeze middle-income Alabama families: What do the candidates for governor plan to do?
items.x: BIRMINGHAM, Ala. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: Daylight saving time ends Sunday: How the time change can impact your mental health
items.x: HARRISONBURG, Va. (WHSV) - As daylight saving time comes to an end early Sunday morning, standard time returns — bringing earlier sunsets, shorter days, and an extra hour of sleep. For many, the annual time shift brings more than just a schedule adjustment. It can trigger feelings of sluggishness, fatigue, and noticeable dips in mood. Holly Humphreys, a licensed professional counselor with Thriveworks, said the shift often disrupts the body’s circadian rhythm, or internal biological clock. “With the daylight hours getting shorter and it getting darker earlier, I do typically see a decline in my clients’ moods around this time of year,” Humphreys said. “Some don’t stay. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Kettering Foundation. Whitehead cited data from the Kettering Foundation and Gallup’s annual national survey of more than 23,000 adults. He said around 14% of the U.S. population strongly embraces Christian nationalism, with just over 16% at least sympathetic to it. That crash is now shining a light on millions of Americans who live or work in “Danger Zones” in close proximity to airports. Although the FAA has established minimum buffers designed to avoid worst-case scenarios when aviation disasters occur, experts say more needs to be done to protect homes and businesses. items.t: Critically Missing Adult Alert issued for Staunton man
items.x: STAUNTON, Va. (WHSV) - The Virginia State Police has issued a Critically Missing Adult Alert for a 56-year-old man last seen in Staunton. According to Virginia State Police, Jeffrey Scott Bennett was last seen at his residence around 8:30 a.m. Thursday, Oct. 29. Police believe Bennett may be traveling near the Blue Ridge Parkway in the Staunton area. He may be driving a green 1995 Toyota T100 pickup truck with Virginia license plate XGG8878. Bennett is described as 5 feet, 10 inches tall and weighing about 180 pounds. He has brown hair and blue eyes. His clothing description is unknown. Authorities say his disappearance poses a credible threat to his health and safety. Anyone with information about Bennett’s whereabouts is asked to contact Staunton Police Department’s 24-hour dispatch at 540-332-3842. More information about the alert is available at Virginia State Police .

items.t: New Market man dies after Rockingham County motorcycle crash
items.x: ROCKINGHAM COUNTY, Va. (WHSV) - A New Market man died Thursday after a motorcycle crash in Rockingham County, according to Virginia State Police. The crash happened Thursday at 10:35 a.m. at the intersection of Spotswood Trail and New Hope Road, involving a 2018 Yamaha motorcycle and a 2026 Toyota pickup truck, according to VSP. The motorcycle was traveling east on Spotswood Trail at a “high rate of speed,” VSP said, when the Toyota pickup tried to cross Spotswood Trail from New Hope Road. The motorcycle hit the side of the pickup, and the rider was ejected into the median, VSP said. VSP identified the motorcyclist as Xavier Smith, 22, of New Market. Smith was taken to Sentara RMH Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead. The driver and passenger of the pickup, who VSP said were both from Pawleys Island, South Carolina, were not injured. VSP continues to investigate the crash.

Plus, we meet a 91-year-old world record holder in track and field proving that staying active has no age limit. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical. A trip to the doctor without a car Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults. Sandbothe was headed to a doctor’s appointment about 25 minutes from their home outside Kansas City. “There’s no buses out here, not in this kind of rural area out here,” Sandbothe said. “It’s so expensive for Uber to take somewhere all the time.” Sandbothe joked that they thought about improvising. “Someti

items.t: How to check water safety before a lake or river outing

items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.t: Dating again? What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. The Aging Untold experts are addressing the topics of sexual health, how it has changed over the years and how to stay protected. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. Troy (4-4, 2-2 Sun Belt Conference) turned the ball over on downs at the Dukes’ 41-yard line to start the game, and Camden Coleman tossed a 2-yard touchdown pass to Corey Scott on fourth-and-goal nine plays later for a 7-0 lead. Coleman fired a 31-yard touchdown pass to Braeden Wisloski and James Madison (7-2, 4-2) led 14-0 after its first two possessions. items.t: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century. This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. items.t: 2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history. With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms. “It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University. Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars. items.t: 71-year-old grandmother missing after going on walk more than 3 weeks ago, police say
items.x: (Gray News) - A 71-year-old New Jersey woman went for a walk more than three weeks ago and hasn’t been seen since. Belinda Prentice was last seen about 6 p.m. Oct. 5 near Bamburgh Court off New Brunswick Road and Willow Avenue in Franklin Township, a press release said. Her granddaughter, Sienna Benjamin, said Prentice had shown signs of cognitive decline in recent years, and the family was working to determine whether she had dementia and to obtain guardianship, People reported. Franklin Township police and the family are urging residents to check doorbell and security cameras for possible sightings. Anyone with information is asked to call the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-2300.

items.t: Halloween decorations disappearing from Valley yards days before holiday
items.x: HARRISONBURG, Va. (WHSV) - Halloween decorations are disappearing from some yards in the valley, leaving homeowners heartbroken as Halloween night is now only two days away. Ross said her priorities include improving neighborhood safety, reinstating a neighborhood watch program and establishing term limits for council members and the mayor. Ross wants to add stop signs in busier neighborhoods, install crosswalks and improve pedestrian safety. Ross also said rebuilding trust between residents and local government is a key goal. The Cleveland Cavaliers had selected James with the first overall pick in that year’s NBA draft. He scores 25 points in his debut against the Sacramento Kings. The Cavaliers lost 106-92.

items.t: JMU, VPAS celebrates 25 Years of caregiver support program

The caregivers community network provides support for caregivers, while also giving students more hands-on experience. Today, the program celebrates 25 years and its long-lasting impact on the community. Merle Mast, founder of CCN, said when creating this program, there were a few needs she was hoping to address. “The population was beginning to age and continues to age, and a lot of family caregivers are giving 24/7 care to their older family member. items.t: 79-year-old man killed after collision with fire truck
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. ( KWCH /Gray News) - A 79-year-old man was killed in a crash involving a fire truck. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump and Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are accusing Democrats of intentionally trying to confuse Alaska voters, after two candidates named Dan Sullivan appeared on the state’s midterm election ballot for U.S. Senate. Trump is among several Republicans criticizing Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, accusing her of perpetuating a fraud on Alaska voters. The New York Times reported Wednesday that campaign staffers for Peltola, a former Alaska congresswoman now running for the U.S. Senate, tried to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. The effort is not illegal. However, the reports have led Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, to order an investigation into alleged election manipulation. Trump commented on the controversy Thursday before leaving for South Carolina. “So nobody’s going to know what to do.

items.t: Baby dies after 15-year-old girl gives birth at elementary school, reports say
items.x: CHICAGO — Authorities are reportedly investigating the death of a baby after a teen girl gave birth at an elementary school in the Chicago area on Wednesday. Chicago police shared that a 15-year-old girl gave birth at Aldridge Elementary School on East 131st Street, but the baby was pronounced dead at the scene. WLS reports that the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office listed the location of the death as 630 E. 131st St. in Chicago, which is the address for Aldridge Elementary School. The teen girl was reportedly in good condition when taken to an area hospital for treatment. Officials from the elementary school did not immediately comment on the situation, WGN reported.

items.t: 16-year-old killed in tractor crash with semi-truck, officials say
items.x: AUDUBON, Iowa ( KCRG /Gray News) - A teen is dead after being thrown from a tractor in a crash with a semi-truck. Iowa State Patrol said it happened Sunday night on Highway 71, just south of Audubon. A crash report said a semi-truck hit the back of the trailer that the tractor was pulling. Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene. The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries. Crash reports showed this was the second farm equipment crash that happened in Audubon County on Sunday. The other crash left a pickup truck driver with serious injuries after it crashed head-on with a combine.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.t: Space heaters under recall after units reportedly catch fire
items.x: (Gray News) - Almost 340,000 space heaters are under recall throughout the United States due to the risk of fire and burns. DREO space heaters model DR-HSH015 were placed under recall on Oct. 29, the Consumer Product Safety Commission reported. About 338,800 units were affected, with an additional 36,300 sold in Canada. They were sold directly through DREO and other sites like Best Buy and Home Depot between Sept. 2025 and Oct. 2026. According to the recall, the affected space heaters can overheat and catch fire. DREO said they received 17 reports of ignition, three resulting in property damage and one burning a person’s hand. Anyone with a recalled unit should stop using the space heater immediately and contact DREO for a free space heater to replace the faulty one. items.t: ‘Star Trek’ actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
items.x: (AP) - Patrick Stewart , the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises, has died. He was 86. Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed. While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of “A Christmas Carol” and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Watch elk live on Virginia wildlife cam

Elk also share the landscape with other wildlife that appear on camera, such as deer and turkeys, the occasional black bear or coyote, and more. The Virginia Elk Cam typically goes live in September; however, this year the elk weren’t spending time in the fields within view of the camera until recently. items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century. This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. items.t: 2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history. With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms. “It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University. Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed. While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene. The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries. Crash reports showed this was the second farm equipment crash that happened in Audubon County on Sunday. The other crash left a pickup truck driver with serious injuries after it crashed head-on with a combine.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. items.t: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age

Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International , said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.x: NEW ORLEANS (WVUE) - Completed around 1752, the Old Ursuline Convent in the French Quarter is said to be the oldest surviving building in the Mississippi River valley. Now the Old Ursuline Convent Museum, there’s a new exhibit marking 300 years since the Ursuline nuns arrived in New Orleans. Sarah Waits, senior archivist at the Archdiocese of New Orleans, said back then, the sisters landed in a developing colony. “It was a wilderness. According to archdiocesan archives, 12 Ursuline nuns came to New Orleans in 1727 and eventually left the French Quarter in 1824. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

According to Stone, the collision occurred when her daughter Autumn was driving home and a moose appeared in the roadway. Stone said she does not believe her daughter had any time to brake. When firefighters arrived, they found a badly damaged vehicle with Autumn trapped inside. It took several crews to cut her out with the Jaws of Life hydraulic rescue tools. Two Michigan nonprofits are working together to help, providing free therapy and service dogs to veterans and first responders. For Tonya and Scott Shea, the mission is personal. items.t: Dry and breezy this afternoon, but Halloween weekend rain is on the way
items.x: NEW ORLEANS (WVUE) - This afternoon is dry across southeast Louisiana and the Mississippi coast, but that dry stretch comes with a catch. Drought conditions, dry fuels, low humidity and light-to-moderate winds keep the fire danger elevated through the rest of today. Keep that in mind if you’re planning any outdoor burning, and obey all burn bans in place. Be extra careful with open flames even if your parish or county doesn’t have a ban. Thin cirrus clouds overhead are leftovers from Tropical Storm Vance out in the eastern Pacific, which is why fog struggled to form this morning. Where skies do clear tonight, patchy fog is possible as temperatures fall toward 52 degrees. Winds turn more easterly late today into Friday and stay that way through the weekend. The family of 21-month-old Nyxailia Hinton said they want answers after she died Tuesday. The Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said she fell and was hit by a car driven by a family friend at a pumpkin patch. However, details have not been given about how or where she fell. “She just lit up the room,” said Peandra Hinton, the child’s mother. “If you were having a bad day, you see Zayla, she’s gonna turn it all around.” Hinton said her daughter was with a babysitter who took her to the pumpkin patch without permission. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International , said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago. Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings. “That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. items.t: Antidepressants: What to know before you decide
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself for weeks or months is different from a bad day. When it starts to affect sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options. For some people, that could include an antidepressant. Start with a conversation with your provider Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone. “Everybody is individualized so you can just talk with your provider,” Rogers said. Rogers said to recognize whether you’re feeling depressed and to look at signs such as loss of sleep, loss of energy or loss of motivation. Some people might also experience a triggering event that starts a downward spiral, which they can’t pull themself out of, she said. “When your quality of life is being affected, then you might want to look into antidepressant therapy,” Rogers said.
