items.t: The barbershop quartet tradition is alive in New Orleans
items.x: NEW ORLEANS ( InvestigateTV ) - On a Mid City evening, a four-part harmony rang out just off Canal Street. The group, Southern Tradition, has been around since 1999. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship. “The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen. Four men with four different careers create one sound. Hansen is a doctor who sings bass. Hansen Eschette is a med tech singing tenor. Joe Jacquat is a civil engineer who sings baritone. Johnnie Oufnac is the only actual barber in this barbershop quartet, singing lead. “Being together for a long time helps us harmonize and understand where the other person is going,” Hansen said. items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide. Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina. It can create serious long-term complications, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, never damage, and amputations. But many people who have the disease may not know it. The CDC estimates around 11 million live with undiagnosed diabetes. “Every day, almost every hour” battle Andrew Tucker has lived with Type 2 diabetes for nearly two decades. items.x: (Gray News) - Kyle Chrisley, son of reality television star Todd Chrisley, has pleaded guilty to resisting arrest in an incident from December 2025. Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. According to Us Magazine , the remaining charges were dismissed. He was arrested Dec. 20 after his wife called police, reportedly saying he was “belligerent.” When police arrived, Chrisley reportedly punched multiple officers . He was arrested and released on an $88,500 bond. People reported that he was arraigned in July before his plea hearing in September.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Owner and Chef Francisco Ortiz said they want to keep things delicious -- and homemade. “We want to bring the best quality in town,” Ortiz said. “One of our goals for this particular location was to provide as much as we can from made from scratch.” You can find Brothers’ Eatery along Holland Drive where they’re open seven days a week.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, says the first group feeling pressure is rural voters. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies. “We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. That’s really changed in the last year, where you see a much more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI,” Borick said. items.t: More than 42 million Americans have cast early midterm ballots
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. items.t: Hometown Hero | Heidi Greenleaf
items.x: ASHLAND, Ky. (WSAZ) - A little greenhouse in Ashland is growing more than just plants. A woman’s love for greenery has turned into a way for neighbors to connect, share and find a little peace in their everyday lives. For owner Heidi Greenleaf, our latest Hometown Hero, it all started with a house full of plants and a simple question. “I thought, how can I share this with other people?” she said. “So, I decided to pop up a free community exchange, very similar to those little free book libraries. And I thought, I really want to do it in our yard, because I’d like to make friends, meet new people, bring community together.” For the full story from Abby Ayes about how that idea grew into something special, check out the video above.

items.t: Courthouse weddings feature Halloween theme
items.x: HUNTINGTON, W.Va. (WSAZ) - Normally, people want their wedding days filled with light colors, a white dress, and flower centerpieces. Some people, though, like to live on the spookier side. On Friday, couples who have a fondness for the Halloween season came to Cabell County Circuit Judge Chad Lovejoy in Huntington to officiate their special day on the holiday. These couples ditched a traditional wedding for one with black tablecloths, a pumpkin balloon, and an orange and black color scheme. “What we do is very, very serious, and so having a day like this, that the community can come in and have a wedding and have some fun and smile is a nice,” Judge Lovejoy said. “It’s one of the nice things that we do.” Judge Lovejoy and his staff really got into the fun, decorating the courtroom for the big day. Altogether, including walkups, they performed about a dozen Halloween weddings on Friday.

items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. items.t: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. items.t: New park name revealed in Proctorville
items.x: LAWRENCE COUNTY, Ohio. (WSAZ) - The name of a new park coming to Proctorville has been announced. In a press conference Friday, the Lawrence County Commissioners said the new park will be named the Todd DeGarmo Park. The name is in honor of its designer, Todd DeGarmo, a former resident of the community. The park is more than 50 acres in the Union/Rome area. The commissioners also announced a recreation plan for all of Lawrence County. The plan seeks to: Identify and leverage the robust natural and cultural assets of Lawrence County. Improve existing public amenities. Propose projects that provide increased access by residents to recreation opportunities. Connect existing and proposed projects through a network of multimodal routes. The commissioners said the recreation plan will receive funding from federal and state programs. More about the recreation plan can be found here .

items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. items.t: Missing man from Texas found dead near train station
items.x: FAYETTE COUNTY, W.Va. (WSAZ) - A missing man was found dead near a train station in Fayette County Thursday, according to the Fayette County Sheriff’s Department. Deputies say they were notified Thursday morning of a missing person report filed in Raleigh County for Paul Kirkland, 35, of Caddo Mills, Texas, and were asked to be on the lookout for him. Around 8 a.m. Thursday, Kirkland was found dead near the Prince Train Station by a CSX employee, deputies say. Deputies say an initial investigation found Kirkland was traveling northbound on Route 41 on a dirt bike sometime Wednesday night when he lost control coming out of a curve near the train tracks. Kirkland was not wearing a helmet, deputies say. Deputies say the crash went undiscovered overnight because Kirkland and debris were located far from the roadway. The incident is still under investigation.

According to Alaska State Troopers, 38-year-old Sasha Hart and her husband, 41-year-old David Hart, were killed in the Oct. 19 crash on the Parks Highway near Trapper Creek. According to troopers, Sasha Hart was driving a Subaru Forester south on the Parks Highway when she crossed the center line and collided head-on with a northbound Ford F-250. Their 2-year-old daughter, Paige, was also in the Subaru and survived. “She’s a miracle. Aren’t you?” Shery Elterman-Hart, David Hart’s sister, said as she held her niece during an interview. A life built in Fairbanks According to the Hart family, the couple just celebrated their 10-year anniversary. items.t: Flags lowered in honor of late deputy
items.x: CHARLESTON, W.Va. (WSAZ) – West Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey on Thursday ordered flags at the Capitol Complex and all state buildings in Logan County to fly at half-staff Friday in honor of the late Deputy Caden Mullins. The Logan County Sheriff’s Office deputy is set to be laid to rest Friday after being killed in a crash involving a coal truck on Oct. 24. Mullins was a Logan County native and a graduate of Man High School.

items.t: Trick-or-treat celebrated at Safety Town
items.x: HUNTINGTON, W.Va. (WSAZ) - Safety remains a priority during the Halloween season, and Thursday’s trick-or-treat event at Safety Town combined that reminder with a fun evening for the family. Huntington Police Department and more than 50 venders and organizations lined the streets of Safety Town to pass out candy to a crowd of costumed kids and their families. One person passing out candy said this type of event is good for the community. “It’s such a great, safe place that people know that they can bring their kids and they don’t have to worry about cars running them down and all kinds of crazy things happening,” Louise Holmes with Roll-A-Rama Skate Center said. “We love doing this. we love being out in the community, and we love Halloween.“ Head to the trick-or-treat tab on WSAZ.com for times and locations across the region.

items.x: HUNTINGTON, W.Va. (WSAZ) - For those looking for a thrill before Halloween, Midvale Haunt is bringing the sights and frights to its front yard. A full list of trick-or-treat times and locations can be found on WSAZ.com.

items.t: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century. This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. items.t: 2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history. With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms. “It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University. Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars. items.t: 71-year-old grandmother missing after going on walk more than 3 weeks ago, police say
items.x: (Gray News) - A 71-year-old New Jersey woman went for a walk more than three weeks ago and hasn’t been seen since. Belinda Prentice was last seen about 6 p.m. Oct. 5 near Bamburgh Court off New Brunswick Road and Willow Avenue in Franklin Township, a press release said. Her granddaughter, Sienna Benjamin, said Prentice had shown signs of cognitive decline in recent years, and the family was working to determine whether she had dementia and to obtain guardianship, People reported. Franklin Township police and the family are urging residents to check doorbell and security cameras for possible sightings. Anyone with information is asked to call the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-2300.

items.t: 79-year-old man killed after collision with fire truck
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. ( KWCH /Gray News) - A 79-year-old man was killed in a crash involving a fire truck. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

Chicago police shared that a 15-year-old girl gave birth at Aldridge Elementary School on East 131st Street, but the baby was pronounced dead at the scene. WLS reports that the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office listed the location of the death as 630 E. 131st St. in Chicago, which is the address for Aldridge Elementary School. items.t: 16-year-old killed in tractor crash with semi-truck, officials say
items.x: AUDUBON, Iowa ( KCRG /Gray News) - A teen is dead after being thrown from a tractor in a crash with a semi-truck. Iowa State Patrol said it happened Sunday night on Highway 71, just south of Audubon. A crash report said a semi-truck hit the back of the trailer that the tractor was pulling. Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene. The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries. Crash reports showed this was the second farm equipment crash that happened in Audubon County on Sunday. The other crash left a pickup truck driver with serious injuries after it crashed head-on with a combine.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies. “We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. According to the University of Florida Election Lab , early midterm turnout is similar to the 2018 “blue wave.” The lab said enthusiasm appears to be on the Democrats’ side. Michael McDonald, a University of Florida political scientist, said the U.S. could be headed toward record turnout. “It’s possible that we will beat the 2018 turnout rate. That was the highest turnout rate for midterm elections since 1914. But there are uneven patterns of turnout,” McDonald said. McDonald said the uneven turnout levels come from a partisan divide. “Registered Democrats, unaffiliated, those people who don’t have a party registration, are engaged at the moment. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. items.x: (Gray News) - A 71-year-old New Jersey woman went for a walk more than three weeks ago and hasn’t been seen since. Belinda Prentice was last seen about 6 p.m. Oct. 5 near Bamburgh Court off New Brunswick Road and Willow Avenue in Franklin Township, a press release said. Her granddaughter, Sienna Benjamin, said Prentice had shown signs of cognitive decline in recent years, and the family was working to determine whether she had dementia and to obtain guardianship, People reported. Franklin Township police and the family are urging residents to check doorbell and security cameras for possible sightings. Anyone with information is asked to call the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-2300.

Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: Trump slams Peltola campaign over two Sullivans on Alaska ballot
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump and Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are accusing Democrats of intentionally trying to confuse Alaska voters, after two candidates named Dan Sullivan appeared on the state’s midterm election ballot for U.S. Senate. Trump is among several Republicans criticizing Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, accusing her of perpetuating a fraud on Alaska voters. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.t: ‘Star Trek’ actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
items.x: (AP) - Patrick Stewart , the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises, has died. He was 86. Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed. While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of “A Christmas Carol” and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen. items.t: The Breakdown: What Happens When El Niño Goes “Super”?
items.x: MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - When meteorologists talk about El Niño, you often hear warnings about shifting jet streams, wetter winters across the South, and unusual severe weather setups. But not all El Niños are created equal. Every once in a rare while, equatorial waters in the central and eastern Pacific heat up to historic, extreme levels—blowing well past standard thresholds and triggering what atmospheric scientists classify as a “Super” El Niño . items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. items.t: Antidepressants: What to know before you decide
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself for weeks or months is different from a bad day. When it starts to affect sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options. For some people, that could include an antidepressant. Start with a conversation with your provider Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone. “Everybody is individualized so you can just talk with your provider,” Rogers said. Rogers said to recognize whether you’re feeling depressed and to look at signs such as loss of sleep, loss of energy or loss of motivation. Some people might also experience a triggering event that starts a downward spiral, which they can’t pull themself out of, she said. “When your quality of life is being affected, then you might want to look into antidepressant therapy,” Rogers said. items.t: Nearly 11 million people in the U.S. could be living with undiagnosed diabetes
items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Belinda Prentice was last seen about 6 p.m. Oct. 5 near Bamburgh Court off New Brunswick Road and Willow Avenue in Franklin Township, a press release said. Her granddaughter, Sienna Benjamin, said Prentice had shown signs of cognitive decline in recent years, and the family was working to determine whether she had dementia and to obtain guardianship, People reported. Franklin Township police and the family are urging residents to check doorbell and security cameras for possible sightings. Anyone with information is asked to call the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-2300.

Senate race ad spending The U.S. Senate race has drawn the most attention in Texas, with candidates Ken Paxton and James Talarico spending millions on ads. The latest Ad-Impact October report shows more than $324 million in total ad spending in the race from May to mid-October. Talarico and PACs supporting him spent about $94 million. Paxton and supporting PACs spent about $230 million. items.t: 79-year-old man killed after collision with fire truck
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. ( KWCH /Gray News) - A 79-year-old man was killed in a crash involving a fire truck. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are accusing Democrats of intentionally trying to confuse Alaska voters, after two candidates named Dan Sullivan appeared on the state’s midterm election ballot for U.S. Senate. Trump is among several Republicans criticizing Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, accusing her of perpetuating a fraud on Alaska voters. items.t: Baby dies after 15-year-old girl gives birth at elementary school, reports say
items.x: CHICAGO — Authorities are reportedly investigating the death of a baby after a teen girl gave birth at an elementary school in the Chicago area on Wednesday. Chicago police shared that a 15-year-old girl gave birth at Aldridge Elementary School on East 131st Street, but the baby was pronounced dead at the scene. WLS reports that the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office listed the location of the death as 630 E. 131st St. in Chicago, which is the address for Aldridge Elementary School. The teen girl was reportedly in good condition when taken to an area hospital for treatment. Officials from the elementary school did not immediately comment on the situation, WGN reported.

items.t: 16-year-old killed in tractor crash with semi-truck, officials say
items.x: AUDUBON, Iowa ( KCRG /Gray News) - A teen is dead after being thrown from a tractor in a crash with a semi-truck. Iowa State Patrol said it happened Sunday night on Highway 71, just south of Audubon. A crash report said a semi-truck hit the back of the trailer that the tractor was pulling. Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene. The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries. Crash reports showed this was the second farm equipment crash that happened in Audubon County on Sunday. The other crash left a pickup truck driver with serious injuries after it crashed head-on with a combine.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. DREO space heaters model DR-HSH015 were placed under recall on Oct. 29, the Consumer Product Safety Commission reported. About 338,800 units were affected, with an additional 36,300 sold in Canada. They were sold directly through DREO and other sites like Best Buy and Home Depot between Sept. 2025 and Oct. 2026. According to the recall, the affected space heaters can overheat and catch fire. Anyone with a recalled unit should stop using the space heater immediately and contact DREO for a free space heater to replace the faulty one. Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed. While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of “A Christmas Carol” and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen. items.x: WACO, Texas (KWTX) - Texas voters will elect a state comptroller on Nov. 3. According to the Texas Comptroller’s office, the comptroller serves as the state’s chief financial officer, serving a four-year term. The office states it collects more than 60 state taxes and fees, pays state bills and employee salaries, and manages the state treasury, including funds totaling more than $150 billion. Every two years, the comptroller issues a biennial revenue estimate, according to the comptroller’s office. The Texas Tribune reports that forecast sets the legal limit for state spending, affecting funding for public schools, roads and tax cuts. According to the comptroller’s office, the office also oversees unclaimed property, college savings plans, state contracts, school vouchers and broadband expansion. items.t: I’m electing you for what? Texas lieutenant governor
items.x: WACO, Texas (KWTX) - Texas voters will elect a lieutenant governor Nov. 3, one of the most powerful jobs in state government. You may think this is a job stuck in the shadow of the governor. But when a big vote happens and it’s a tie, this person decides yay or nay. That’s because the lieutenant governor is president of the Texas Senate, according to the Texas Constitution and the Texas Senate. The office picks Senate committee members and chairs and co-chairs boards that shape the state budget, plus coordinates public education policy and funding, according to the Office of the Lieutenant Governor and the Texas Senate. Should the governor not be able to serve, temporarily or permanently, the lieutenant governor steps in and fills the role until the chief returns or until the elected term ends, according to the Texas Constitution. items.x: WACO, Texas (KWTX) - Texas voters will elect a governor Nov. 3 to serve as chief executive of the state. The governor is elected by citizens every four years, according to the Office of the Texas Governor. The governor must be at least 30 years old and a resident of Texas for the five years immediately before the election. The governor makes policy recommendations that lawmakers in the state House and Senate may sponsor and introduce as bills. The governor also appoints the secretary of state, as well as members of boards and commissions who oversee the heads of state agencies and departments. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. items.t: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — Gen Z carries more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even after adjusting for inflation, according to TransUnion data cited by a credit counseling expert. Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International , said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago. Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings. “That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. items.t: Kyle Chrisley pleads guilty to charges stemming from 2025 arrest, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Kyle Chrisley, son of reality television star Todd Chrisley, has pleaded guilty to resisting arrest in an incident from December 2025. Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. items.t: Wilmington community unites for annual Out of the Darkness Walk
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. (WECT) - The annual Wilmington Area Out of the Darkness Community Walk returns this weekend, bringing the community together to raise awareness for suicide prevention and mental health support. The non-competitive walk directly supports research, advocacy efforts and educational programs across the state. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Oak Island’s Veterans Park gets makeover from local Lowe’s employees
items.x: OAK ISLAND, N.C. (WECT) - Employees from the Southport and Shallotte Lowe’s Home Improvement stores volunteered their time at Veterans Park in Oak Island Friday. The volunteers pressure washed, planted trees and shrubs, built retaining walls and put up new flags. The park will have a new look by sunset. Many of the volunteers are veterans, including Lowe’s Randy Modlin. Modlin said one volunteer stood out. “We actually had one gentleman here today named Andy. He’s a veteran, got a lot of disabilities and stuff like that, but he came out and gave two hours of his time today,” Modlin said. The project aims to remind veterans across the community that they have not been forgotten.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Experts eye key voting blocs ahead of Midterms
items.x: NEW YORK CITY (Gray Media) - With millions of ballots already cast ahead of Election Day, conversations surrounding voter turnout are intensifying. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Lincoln Mitchell, a political analyst and professor at Columbia University, says the first group feeling pressure is rural voters. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.t: How AI is impacting the midterm elections
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As midterm candidates begin to make their final pitches to voters, experts are speaking out about the impact of artificial intelligence on this election cycle. Chris Borick, a political science professor at Lehigh University, said AI has become a major issue in several races in the last few months. He noted how different the rhetoric surrounding it has been compared to other new technologies. “We like tech traditionally as part of our political economy. That’s really changed in the last year, where you see a much more neutral and sometimes negative political position on AI,” Borick said. items.t: Trump to make final midterm stops in Iowa and Kansas Sunday
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump will make final campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, two days before Tuesday’s midterm elections. Trump won Iowa three times and Kansas twice. He is hoping to give Republicans a final boost in both states. He originally scrapped the stops but decided at the last minute to go through with them. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: Drivers to face lane closures for bridge work on N.C. 53
items.x: PENDER COUNTY, N.C. (WECT) - Travelers heading through a stretch of N.C. 53 should prepare for traffic delays as state transportation crews begin bridge upkeep. Up-to-date traffic conditions are available online and through North Carolina Department of Transportation social media channels.

items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. Start with the question the trial is trying to answer Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to change the question you ask. “I think the first thing we have to do is not think about, ‘Can this clinical trial help me?’ but ‘What is this clinical trial trying to answer?’” Rogers said. “That’s what most of these trials are about.” A trial is not a last resort Rogers said many people see clinical trials as a last resort. “I think a lot of people think that it’s a last resort option, that you don’t have anything else, when in fact one of th

items.t: US 17 Southbound closed in Shallotte following major crash
items.x: SHALLOTTE, N.C. (WECT) - A collision involving an overturned box truck and a jackknifed tractor-trailer has shut down southbound traffic on U.S. 17 in Shallotte, according to authorities. WECT crews at the scene say Highway 17 is blocked at Old Shallotte Road. Authorities urge drivers to avoid the area, find alternate routes and prepare for delays. Motorists traveling through the surrounding area are asked to slow down and use caution to give emergency crews sufficient room to work.

items.t: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. items.t: How art therapy helps patients connect with caregivers
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. June said the first signs that something was wrong appeared in 2019, starting with forgetfulness and then repeating tasks. Cognitive testing later confirmed their fears. items.t: Pet of the Week: Meet Tiana from Paws Place Dog Rescue
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. (WECT) - A 1 1/2-year-old shepherd mix named Tiana is waiting to meet her forever family at Paws Place Dog Rescue. Staff describe Tiana as an energetic, affectionate companion who knows tricks and enjoys splashing around in the facility’s doggie pool. She is equally comfortable joining a multi-dog household or thriving as an only pet, and rescue workers say she gets along well with both adults and children. Those interested in adopting can visit the rescue facility at 242 George II Highway in Winnabow. Walk-ins are welcome Tuesday through Saturday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., with no appointment necessary. For more details on the adoption process, call Paws Place Dog Rescue at 910-845-7297.

items.t: BIG WIN: Wilmington Army veteran wins over $76K on ‘Wheel of Fortune’
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. (WECT) - A Wilmington man walked away with a massive payday after dominating the Bonus Round on ‘Wheel of Fortune’ Thursday night. Randolph “Moe” Moultrie claimed more than $76,000 in cash and prizes, including a getaway trip to Mexico, during the Oct. 29 Halloween-themed episode. Moultrie, an Army veteran, father of three and healthcare worker, grew up watching the iconic game show with his grandfather and described his appearance as a tribute to their bond. Over 100 friends, family members and community supporters gathered Thursday night at Four Corners Wrightsville Beach to celebrate the win and watch Moultrie solve his way to the winner’s circle.

items.t: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century. This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. items.t: 2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history. With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms. “It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University. Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars. items.t: 71-year-old grandmother missing after going on walk more than 3 weeks ago, police say
items.x: (Gray News) - A 71-year-old New Jersey woman went for a walk more than three weeks ago and hasn’t been seen since. Belinda Prentice was last seen about 6 p.m. Oct. 5 near Bamburgh Court off New Brunswick Road and Willow Avenue in Franklin Township, a press release said. Her granddaughter, Sienna Benjamin, said Prentice had shown signs of cognitive decline in recent years, and the family was working to determine whether she had dementia and to obtain guardianship, People reported. Franklin Township police and the family are urging residents to check doorbell and security cameras for possible sightings. Anyone with information is asked to call the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-2300.

items.t: 79-year-old man killed after collision with fire truck
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. ( KWCH /Gray News) - A 79-year-old man was killed in a crash involving a fire truck. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

I still get to do what I want to do. I still get to go where I want to go,” he said. Smith was diagnosed after a series of scans and blood tests. His story goes back almost 10 years, when he noticed his mind was starting to decline and got tested. Smith described the moment he learned of the diagnosis. “For the first time in a long time, it felt like I had a tear running down my eye... She turned around from her screen and said, ‘You’ve got Alzheimer’s,’” Smith said. Over 7 million Americans share Smith’s reality. items.t: World Stroke Day: Former firefighter turns stroke survival into lifelong mission of hope
items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. (WECT) - For more than three decades, William “Bill” Blenk was the person running toward danger, saving lives as a firefighter and training the next generation as an EMT instructor. But 21 years ago, life flipped in an instant when he became the one who needed saving. He was 64 when a stroke took away his ability to do the simplest daily tasks. “I could not talk. I could not write. I could not eat. I had to learn how to eat,” he said. His wife, Pat, said she still remembers the terrifying moment it started. “He said, ‘Pat, Pat, something’s gravely wrong.’ I said, ‘What’s wrong?’ And then he had the weakness starting. And when we got to the hospital, he couldn’t talk,” she said. Faced with a sudden silence, Pat found a way to bridge the gap. items.t: Fire officials say commercial building fire near Shallotte not related to other fires
items.x: SHALLOTTE, N.C. (WECT) - A fire at Ike’s Pit off Old Georgetown Road took more than four hours to bring under control Wednesday evening. [PREVIOUS STORY: Fire off Old Georgetown Road in Brunswick County under control] The Shallotte Point Volunteer Fire Department responded around 6:30 p.m. Fire Department Chief Buddy Causey said welding equipment stored inside the building caused several explosions as the fire burned. Blasts could be heard in the area and smoke filled the sky. “There were a few explosions,” Causey said. “[The owner] had welding equipment and stuff inside the building, so some of the bottles were exploding inside the building during the fire.” Officials said the fire was unrelated to previous fires in the area or to the large wildfires earlier this year. Workers at Ike’s Pit declined an on-camera interview. No injuries were reported.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: Trump slams Peltola campaign over two Sullivans on Alaska ballot
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - President Donald Trump and Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are accusing Democrats of intentionally trying to confuse Alaska voters, after two candidates named Dan Sullivan appeared on the state’s midterm election ballot for U.S. Senate. Trump is among several Republicans criticizing Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola, accusing her of perpetuating a fraud on Alaska voters. The New York Times reported Wednesday that campaign staffers for Peltola, a former Alaska congresswoman now running for the U.S. Senate, tried to recruit a candidate with the same name as Republican Sen. items.x: CHICAGO — Authorities are reportedly investigating the death of a baby after a teen girl gave birth at an elementary school in the Chicago area on Wednesday. Chicago police shared that a 15-year-old girl gave birth at Aldridge Elementary School on East 131st Street, but the baby was pronounced dead at the scene. items.t: 16-year-old killed in tractor crash with semi-truck, officials say
items.x: AUDUBON, Iowa ( KCRG /Gray News) - A teen is dead after being thrown from a tractor in a crash with a semi-truck. Iowa State Patrol said it happened Sunday night on Highway 71, just south of Audubon. A crash report said a semi-truck hit the back of the trailer that the tractor was pulling. Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene. The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries. The Seniors’ Health Insurance Information Program (SHIIP) is leading the presentation at 7 p.m. on Nov. 5 at the Kure Beach Community Center. SHIIP counselors will give an overview of Medicare Parts A, B and D. They will also explain Medicare Advantage and Medicare Supplement plans. items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.t: Space heaters under recall after units reportedly catch fire

Besides playing everyone from Claudius to Macbeth, he often performed a one-man rendition of “A Christmas Carol” and did West End and Broadway runs of Harold Pinter’s “No Man’s Land” and Samuel Beckett’s “Waiting for Godot” in repertoire with buddy Ian McKellen. items.t: NC Attorney General wins federal lawsuit blocking Medicaid rule for seriously ill
items.x: RALEIGH, N.C. (WECT) - A federal judge has struck down a Medicaid rule that threatened to strip health coverage from an estimated 64,000 seriously ill North Carolinians. Attorney General Jeff Jackson sued the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services in June after a new rule made it harder for seriously ill patients to keep their Medicaid coverage. Under the new rule, cancer patients on chemotherapy would have had to prove they were seriously ill and unable to work 80 hours a month. Jackson argued that CMS exceeded its authority by narrowing an exemption created by Congress. On Oct. 29, U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns ruled in favor of Jackson, stating that CMS overstepped its authority. items.t: ‘I rape little girls like you’: Former councilman arrested after allegedly making terrorist threats at Hooters

items.t: Henry’s House brings relief to North Carolina caregivers
items.x: BURGAW, N.C. (WECT) - A new facility designed to give caregivers a temporary break while supporting youth with complex needs is opening in Pender County. Henry’s House, located at 314 Progress Drive in Burgaw, offers care for children and young adults ages 6 to 21 diagnosed with developmental disabilities and other complex needs. The facility features six single-occupancy rooms and offers recreational and skill-building activities tailored to each person’s interests and abilities. Chrisley was arrested on charges including assault on a police officer, disorderly conduct, domestic assault, public intoxication and resisting arrest. According to Us Magazine , the remaining charges were dismissed.
