items.t: Dog rescued from ledge in Wolfe County
items.x: WOLFE COUNTY, Ky. (WKYT) - The Wolfe County Search & Rescue Team came to the aid of man’s best friend Thursday. The team was called to the Big Bend Road area in Wolfe County around 7 p.m. after someone reported that two dogs had fallen off a cliff and were stranded on a small ledge. When the team arrived in the area, the team was only able to locate one dog. A team member was lowered to the ledge, but the dog displayed aggressive behavior. After what the team called a peace offering of hot dogs and beef jerky, the dog was pacified enough to be leashed and brought off the ledge. The dog has since been named Lucky and will soon be put up for adoption at the Wolfe County Animal Shelter.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. items.t: Kentucky early voting numbers rise significantly
items.x: KENTUCKY (WKYT) - The number of early voters for the Democratic and Republican parties in Kentucky has jumped significantly in the last four years, according to data released Friday by Secretary of State Michael Adams. Through Thursday, 95,645 registered Democrats had already voted. That number is nearly triple the 37,640 who did so in 2022. For Republicans, 83,726 party members have already cast their ballots. That is more than double the number from four years ago, when 39,349 voted early. The number of early voters who are independent tripled. In 2022, 4,392 voted early. This year, that number is 12,579. items.t: Kentucky’s longest serving congressman says he’s confident about re-election bid

items.t: FIRST ALERT FORECAST: Ending October on a Dry Note
items.x: HAZARD, Ky. (WYMT) - Alright, here’s what’s happening as we wrap up Friday. A dry cold front is working its way south toward the Tennessee border. This isn’t your typical strong cold front. This one’s moisture-starved and weak. The main thing it does is change the wind direction from southerly to northeasterly tonight. Otherwise, we’re still riding high pressure and staying dry through Saturday. Tonight’s Situation That cold front will continue sagging south through eastern Kentucky over the next few hours and should reach the Tennessee border by late evening. Behind it, north to northeast winds develop. We’ll see some valley fog possible in the deeper hollows and low-lying areas tonight, mainly along the Kentucky, Big Sandy, and Cumberland basins. items.t: Aging Untold: When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we address how aging and illness can impact intimacy, sharing practical ways for couples to talk openly and safely navigate sex after a diagnosis. Then, we discuss clinical trials, why older adults are frequently underrepresented and what questions to ask before participating in a study. Plus, we meet a 91-year-old world record holder in track and field proving that staying active has no age limit. When health changes your sex life, intimacy doesn’t have to disappear Health can affect intimacy as we age and the Aging Untold experts are addressing questions many couples are afraid to ask out loud: When is it safe to resume sex? What if it isn’t? And what should you ask your doctor? Sam Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first step is figuring out what’s behind the change. (Gray News) - A 21-year-old woman was arrested after allegedly posting a photo of herself with a caption that she was going to shoot President Trump. “We are not going to tolerate threats to assassinate the president,” the Volusia County Sheriff Mike Chitwood wrote in a social media post on Oct. 30. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: Malachi Moreno Tabbed to Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Center of the Year Preseason Watch List
items.x: LEXINGTON, Ky. (WYMT) - University of Kentucky sophomore center Malachi Moreno was named Friday to the 2026-27 Kareem Abdul-Jabbar Center of the Year preseason watch list, the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame announced. Moreno is one of 20 players nationally selected for the preseason list, which has honored the top center in Division I men’s basketball each season since 2015. The Georgetown, Kentucky, native enters his second year with the Wildcats after earning All-Southeastern Conference Freshman Team honors last season. Moreno started 30 games as a freshman, averaging 7.8 points and a team-high 6.3 rebounds while shooting 58.2% from the floor. He also led Kentucky with 53 blocks, recorded 11 double-digit scoring games, posted three double-doubles and averaged 1.8 assists per game. items.t: 103 year-old skydiver
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - A woman in Ohio is proving you can do anything, at any age. At 103-years-old she jumped out of a plane and set the record for the oldest person to ever go skydiving in Ohio.

items.t: 4 hospitalized after lightning strike at elementary school
items.x: EL MIRAGE, Ariz. ( KPHO /Gray News) — Authorities in Arizona say several adults were injured by a lightning strike at an elementary school bus drop-off Friday morning. First responders said they were called just after 8:30 a.m. for reports of a lightning strike at El Mirage Elementary School. Four people, all identified as adults, were conscious and taken to a nearby hospital for treatment, according to the El Mirage Police Department. El Mirage Fire Captain Joseph Rivera said one woman was holding an umbrella when lightning struck in the vicinity. The woman reported feeling pain in both of her arms. Capt. Rivera said none of the people were directly struck by the lightning. items.t: Magic water fountain

But what about those kids who bring character, joy, understanding? Our Chad Douglas takes us to a place where teachers use a little whimsy to catapult more students into the spotlight.

items.t: Twiggy, the water skiing squirrel

The Best family conceived of the idea after they rescued a squirrel that was blown from its nest after a storm. One remote control boat, a willing squirrel, and lots of practice launched this amazing act.

items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical. A trip to the doctor without a car Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults. Sandbothe was headed to a doctor’s appointment about 25 minutes from their home outside Kansas City. “There’s no buses out here, not in this kind of rural area out here,” Sandbothe said. “It’s so expensive for Uber to take somewhere all the time.” Sandbothe joked that they thought about improvising. “Someti

items.t: How to check water safety before a lake or river outing
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — A new report from Environment America found bacteria levels were potentially unsafe on at least one day at 69% of more than 4,500 river and lake testing locations in 17 states. John Rumpler, clean water director and senior attorney at Environment America, said the group’s “Safe for Swimming” report matters as a consumer issue as well as an environmental one. “I can only imagine that if a family drove two or three hours to go to lakeside cabin, and they were planning to spend the entire week at the lake, and then suddenly there was E. coli in the water,” Rumpler said. “I don’t know that I could put that to dollars and cents, but I think we might agree that’s a ruined vacation right there.” Rumpler said E. coli turned up in every state in the analysis. “All across the country in all of these 17 states, we found E. coli, which people may be familiar with E. coli as a nas

items.t: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. (WYMT) - The three men charged in connection to the murder of Amber Spradlin appeared in Pike Circuit Court Friday as attorneys prepare for the highly anticipated January trial. items.t: Customers suffer chemical burns after drinking margaritas at a NC Chili’s, officials say
items.x: FOREST CITY, N.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths. Health officials investigating the incident at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina, said the drinks were contaminated after a powerful industrial degreaser was mistaken for sugar. The dangerous mix-up began when a restaurant worker obtained granulated degreasing agent from an outside contractor power-washing the building’s exterior, according to the Foothills Health District. The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. items.t: Mayor: Medical emergency caused City of Hazard employee to crash into building
items.x: HAZARD, Ky. (WYMT/WKYT) - Mayor Donald “Happy” Mobelini of Hazard confirmed that a medical emergency led a city employee to crash into a building. Police and paramedics were called to the former France’s Diner in downtown Hazard after a truck crashed into the building Friday morning. According to the building’s owner, the truck was owned and operated by the City of Hazard. The truck slammed into the building around 9:15 a.m. There was no one inside the building at the time of impact. Mayor Mobelini confirmed that the employee suffered an emergency and was taken to a local hospital following the crash. The employee was then transported to UK Hospital. His name and condition has not been released.

items.t: Dating again? What older adults should know about sexual health and protection
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. The Aging Untold experts are addressing the topics of sexual health, how it has changed over the years and how to stay protected. You can’t tell by looking Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said appearances do not show whether someone has a sexually transmitted disease. “You can’t tell by looking at someone if they have a sexually transmitted disease,” Rogers said. “You say, ‘Oh, they look healthy.’ You can’t tell by that.” She said age does not change that risk. “Getting older does not make you immune to getting a sexually transmitted disease,” Rogers said. “Just because you retired, your sexual health didn’t.” Rogers said older adults have to

items.t: Ground cinnamon recalled ahead of holiday season due to elevated lead risk, FDA says
items.x: (Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season. SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert. The affected cinnamon was sold in retail and grocery stores between Sept. 8, 2025, and June 28, 2026, in Connecticut, Indiana, Kansas, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, North Carolina, Nebraska, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Texas, Virginia and Wisconsin. According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.t: ‘Bad houseguest’ in the attic: What to know about shingles symptoms and treatments
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: This family runs a distillery in an old fire station
items.x: DALE, Wis. ( InvestigateTV ) — A Wisconsin family runs a distillery in an old fire station along Highway 96 in Dale, with a business designed to support the fire departments that keep them safe. Volunteer firefighter Alex Hopfensperger works at the family business, Old Station 31 Spirits. “Right now we’re distilling in-house vodka and gin, so we have the four vodkas and two gins,” Alex Hopfensperger said. “We wanted to become a part of the community, and 20-plus years ago, part of becoming part of the community was joining the volunteer fire department,” Rob Hopfensperger said. Alex’s father, Rob, is also a volunteer firefighter. He and his wife, Tavia, decided to honor the fire service when they created Old Station 31 Spirits. “You start to do it and, you know, I’m on it, then your sons get on it, your daughter-in-law gets on it, and it’s just, and we have that,” Rob said. “Living in a

Students in Susan Meunier’s new leadership class are tracing and painting portraits of pets. Vaughn Wurtz and her classmates are working on the project at the school. “We had to do a project for something to do with the community that benefits the community,” Wurtz said. Aubrey Salm and Paul Reinke helped come up with the idea. “We’re doing pet portraits for Go Fetch and we’re going to donate all of the money to the humane society,” Salm said. Meunier said the students are working hard on the portraits. “They are putting so much effort into it,” Meunier said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. How the discovery happened Dr. Cuthbert Simpkins, founder of Vivacelle Bio, said he was running an experiment he thought would fail. “But it didn’t fail.” For years, Simpkins, who is now a surgery professor at the UKMC School of Medicine, had been trying to find an answer for septic shock and focused his research on blood experiments. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. Start with the question the trial is trying to answer Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the first step is to change the question you ask. “I think the first thing we have to do is not think about, ‘Can this clinical trial help me?’ but ‘What is this clinical trial trying to answer?’” Rogers said. “That’s what most of these trials are about.” A trial is not a last resort Rogers said many people see clinical trials as a last resort. “I think a lot of people think that it’s a last resort option, that you don’t have anything else, when in fact one of th

items.t: Bringing cancer screening conversations to the salon chair
items.x: ANDRESON, S.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Do you only go to the doctor when you have an ache or feel sick? For many women that answer can be “yes.” A 2025 survey said that every one in six women say they missed or may have missed a routine cancer screening within the past year. A South Carolina salon is partnering with a statewide health initiative to have important conversations about cancer screening with clients. Kimberly Cheatham, owner of Kreative Kimistry in Anderson, has joined the Pink Palmetto Project, an effort by the South Carolina Cancer Alliance focusing on breast and cervical cancer education. Cheatham said her clients often get personal with her. “They confide in me when they don’t even feel comfortable telling their families things and their friends, because they know that I have a connection to them,” Cheatham said. items.x: WILMINGTON, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) — Some doctors and caregivers are using art to help people with memory loss stay calm, engaged and connected. Research published by the National Library of Medicine shows drawing and painting can sometimes stimulate memories in people with dementia and other neurological diseases. Mother and daughter paint together June Lederle and her daughter, Cathie Lederle, create artwork at a table in their Wilmington home most days. On the day of the interview, Cathie was painting a bottle purple, the color of Alzheimer’s awareness. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. items.t: Bat Week highlights furry fliers’ importance to Kentucky
items.x: FRANKFORT, Ky. (WKYT) - It is Bat Week in Kentucky, with the Kentucky Cabinet for Health and Family Services celebrating the benefits of having bats around and what to do if you come across one. Bats are flying mammals commonly associated with Halloween and vampires, but the bats in Kentucky do not feed on blood. Bats eat insects. Michaela Rogers, a wildlife biologist with the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife, said all the state’s bats are insectivorous, meaning they eat bugs. “One of the main things that people think of them for is a really natural pest control,” Rogers said. “They go out every evening, and they’re going to be eating their weight in insects every single night, so that not only helps us with the bugs around our yards that we may not like as much, but also farmers with pest controls, that sort of thing.” Where bats live There are 15 bat species native to Kentucky.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

Gayle Manning (R-North Ridgeville) sponsored the measure after the Lorain Police Department approached her about an incident where an officer faced intense, nationwide backlash online despite being cleared of any wrongdoing. “They were found they had not done anything wrong, but then that information goes viral,” Manning said. “And all of a sudden, because of social media, it was all over the United States.” Under the proposed legislation, it would be illegal to publicly disclose an officer’s personal identifying information—such as a home address, birth date, or phone number—with the intent to intimidate, threaten, or cause physical harm. items.t: Doctor says time outdoors can support physical and mental health
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.t: Arraignment for former Northeast Ohio high school band director indicted by grand jury
items.x: STARK COUNTY, Ohio (WOIO) — The former band director at Northwest High School in Canal Fulton was arraigned in Stark County Court of Common Pleas Friday. Stephen Imler pleaded not guilty to three charges of sexual battery and one charge of grooming. The judge set bond at $200,000 and ordered Imler to return to court on Nov. 12. Imler, who was also a music teacher at the high school, was placed on administrative leave on Aug. 18 when the allegations were first announced. On Sept. 2, Imler officially resigned from both positions. He was arrested by members of the U.S. Marshals Northern Ohio Violent Fugitive Task Force on Oct. 23. According to U.S. Marshal Pete Elliott, Imler was taken into custody without incident at a home in the 4600 block of Hametown Rd. in Norton.

( WHNS /Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths. Health officials investigating the incident at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina, said the drinks were contaminated after a powerful industrial degreaser was mistaken for sugar. The dangerous mix-up began when a restaurant worker obtained granulated degreasing agent from an outside contractor power-washing the building’s exterior, according to the Foothills Health District. The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.x: COLUMBUS, Ohio (AP) — Ohio governor candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial attack ad featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Dr. Amy Acton, is off the air after the Republican spent about a quarter of what his campaign initially said it would invest to run it. Ramaswamy said during a campaign appearance in Vandalia, Ohio, on Thursday that the ad’s planned run was over. His campaign originally said it would spend $4 million to air the ad, but data from the ad-tracking firm AdImpact showed it spent roughly $1 million. The divisive spot had provoked backlash in Ohio and among politicians of both parties across the nation. It featured Donna Arthur calling her daughter a lifelong liar. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. items.t: Adams County deputy, suspect shot, flown to hospital: Sheriff
items.x: ADAMS COUNTY, Ohio (WXIX) - An Adams County deputy and a suspect were shot Thursday night and flown to a hospital in Cincinnati, according to Adams County Sheriff Kenny Dick. Deputies were called to Hope Lane in West Union around 9:25 p.m. for the report of a mental health-related incident, the sheriff said. Investigators say a suspect opened fire when deputies arrived. They fired back, and both the deputy and the suspect were shot. The deputy and the suspect were taken to the University of Cincinnati Medical Center, the sheriff said. The extent of their injuries is unknown, the sheriff said early Friday. The Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation is investigating. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. Rather than looking solely at party affiliation, political insiders are closely watching three specific demographic groups that could ultimately decide which party controls Congress. Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are accusing Democrats of intentionally trying to confuse Alaska voters, after two candidates named Dan Sullivan appeared on the state’s midterm election ballot for U.S. Senate. Dan S. Sullivan. The effort is not illegal. However, the reports have led Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, to order an investigation into alleged election manipulation. items.t: Baby dies after 15-year-old girl gives birth at elementary school, reports say
items.x: CHICAGO — Authorities are reportedly investigating the death of a baby after a teen girl gave birth at an elementary school in the Chicago area on Wednesday. Chicago police shared that a 15-year-old girl gave birth at Aldridge Elementary School on East 131st Street, but the baby was pronounced dead at the scene. WLS reports that the Cook County Medical Examiner’s Office listed the location of the death as 630 E. 131st St. in Chicago, which is the address for Aldridge Elementary School. The teen girl was reportedly in good condition when taken to an area hospital for treatment. Officials from the elementary school did not immediately comment on the situation, WGN reported.

items.x: AUDUBON, Iowa ( KCRG /Gray News) - A teen is dead after being thrown from a tractor in a crash with a semi-truck. Iowa State Patrol said it happened Sunday night on Highway 71, just south of Audubon. A crash report said a semi-truck hit the back of the trailer that the tractor was pulling. Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene. The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries. Crash reports showed this was the second farm equipment crash that happened in Audubon County on Sunday. The other crash left a pickup truck driver with serious injuries after it crashed head-on with a combine.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. items.t: Jackson fire chief warns residents as fires continue under burn ban
items.x: JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) — Most of the state, including Hinds County, is under a burn ban, but a string of fires has broken out across the city of Jackson. The Jackson Fire Department said the city has seen an influx of fires in the past few weeks and is asking residents to help prevent them. Some of the fires are being investigated as arson, and officials said others started because of simple carelessness. Officials said that under the current burn ban, even a small spark can lead to a felony charge. Jackson Fire Chief RaSean O. Thomas said people are responsible for the fires they cause. “If you throw a cigarette butt out of the window, and you cause a fire, you can burn someone’s home, you can burn someone’s property,” Thomas said. “… That is part of your responsibility to make sure you dispose of it properly. But if you do not and you cause a fire, you’re responsible for that as well.”

Economic headwinds, including agricultural tariffs and the rising cost of everyday essentials like home heating and diesel, are pinching household budgets in rural communities. While Mitchell does not expect these voters to dramatically flip parties, financial strain could depress turnout or weaken enthusiasm for Republicans and President Donald Trump. items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - More than 42 million Americans have cast midterm ballots, and interesting demographic data shows who is voting. items.t: MDOT reports more than 4,200 deer-related crashes in Mississippi in 2025
items.x: JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) — Mississippi reported 4,221 deer-related crashes in 2025, a 6% increase from the 3,960 crashes reported in 2024, according to the Mississippi Department of Transportation (MDOT). MDOT is reminding motorists to watch for deer as the animals become more active during the fall and winter months. Madison County had the most deer-related crashes in Mississippi over the past decade, with 2,437. DeSoto County ranked second with 2,341. Deer activity typically peaks from October through January, but collisions can happen throughout the year. MDOT recommends motorists take extra precautions during early morning and evening hours, when deer are more active. About 20% of deer-related crashes happen in the early morning, while more than half occur between 5 p.m. and midnight. items.t: 91-year-old track and field world record holder continues to compete
items.x: SHELBURNE, Vt. ( Aging Untold ) — Flo Meiler began competing in track and field at age 60. She is now 91 and holds two world records, in the pole vault and triple jump. Medals fill Meiler’s home in Shelburne. Most are gold, and a few are silver. How she started Meiler began competing at 60 when her friend Barbara Jordan convinced her to try the long jump at the Vermont Senior Games, and Meiler was hooked. Jordan died a decade ago. “I miss her so much,” Meiler said. Still competing at 91 Meiler continues to compete. “I’m sad that I can’t jump like I used to, but I really enjoy it,” she said. Meiler said it lifts her up when other athletes approach her and tell her she inspires them. “I really feel really warm inside because I’ve had so many athletes come up to me and say, ‘What an inspiration you have been to me,’” she said. “That’s a wonderful feeling.” Inspiring others One of the people

items.t: 2 people, 5 dogs rescued from Olive Branch house fire
items.x: OLIVE BRANCH, Miss. (WMC) - Two people and five dogs were rescued Thursday night after a house fire broke out along Oak Leaf Drive. The Olive Branch Fire Department responded to the home around 7 p.m. When crews arrived, they helped an elderly woman and two dogs safely evacuate. The woman was transported to a local hospital for evaluation. Firefighters then entered the home, encountering heavy smoke and flames spreading through the kitchen and living room. During a search, crews located a elderly man trapped inside a back bathroom. He was rushed to Regional One Health and treated for smoke inhalation and esophageal burns; officials expect him to make a full recovery. Firefighters also found three more dogs inside the house, rescuing and treating them on scene. Investigators determined the fire started in the kitchen, though the exact cause remains under investigation. Click here to sign

Four people, all identified as adults, were conscious and taken to a nearby hospital for treatment, according to the El Mirage Police Department. El Mirage Fire Captain Joseph Rivera said one woman was holding an umbrella when lightning struck in the vicinity. The woman reported feeling pain in both of her arms. Capt. Rivera said none of the people were directly struck by the lightning. items.t: New study reveals 43% drop in childhood peanut allergies over last decade
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Recent research suggests that the long-held medical advice to avoid peanut products for young children may have been exactly the wrong approach. New studies indicate that introducing peanut products to infants between 4 and 6 months old can significantly reduce the risk of developing a peanut allergy. According to a study released in October 2025, peanut allergy rates in children under 3 have dropped by roughly 43% over the last decade. Dr. David Hill, lead author of the study, believes the reversal in guidance is a major factor in this decline. “It’s safe to say in all likelihood, there are tens of thousands of kids today that don’t have food allergy that may have if we hadn’t made these recommendations about early allergen introduction,” Dr. Hill said. items.t: Older adults who stop driving face transportation gaps, experts say
items.x: KANSAS CITY ( InvestigateTV ) — As people age and their health changes, families can face the question of when a loved one should stop driving. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration reports older drivers are more likely than younger drivers to be involved in a car accident. They are “more likely to be seriously hurt,” according to the agency. Most older drivers do not have a plan for when they can no longer drive, which aging experts say is critical. A trip to the doctor without a car Kennie Sandbothe, 77, stopped driving and now relies on a ride program for older adults. Sandbothe was headed to a doctor’s appointment about 25 minutes from their home outside Kansas City. “There’s no buses out here, not in this kind of rural area out here,” Sandbothe said. “It’s so expensive for Uber to take somewhere all the time.” Sandbothe joked that they thought about improvising. “Someti

items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Spending time in nature can be a healthy reset, according to a doctor who also practices wilderness medicine. Dr. Nathaniel Mann, a Prisma Health emergency doctor, said time spent outdoors is one of the most powerful treatments he has seen, and he supports prescribing it. “Humans, we really didn’t evolve to live in these big structured communities with all the traffic and lights and noise. Our genetic roots are in the outdoors and the surroundings that we see around us right now,” Mann said. Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.x: FOREST CITY, N.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) – A round of drinks turned into a medical nightmare when three customers ordered margaritas and immediately suffered chemical burns inside and around their mouths. Health officials investigating the incident at a Chili’s Grill & Bar in Forest City, North Carolina, said the drinks were contaminated after a powerful industrial degreaser was mistaken for sugar. The dangerous mix-up began when a restaurant worker obtained granulated degreasing agent from an outside contractor power-washing the building’s exterior, according to the Foothills Health District. The employee poured the chemical into an unlabeled container, brought it inside and left it in the bar area. items.x: JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) - Revenue continues to go up, but it is still not enough to cover JXN Water’s monthly expenses. Even with the increase and other cost controls implemented, JXN Water is about $2.7 million over budget on the year. The utility is staying afloat, in part, due to a $54 million grant that was reallocated as part of a November 2025 Congressional act. items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Dating, intimacy and connection can be an important part of emotional and physical well-being for older adults. That includes people who are divorced, widowed, remarried or dating again for the first time in decades. items.x: (Gray News) - Ground cinnamon is being recalled in 14 states ahead of the holiday season. SLR Food Distribution Inc said it’s voluntarily recalling Wise Wife Brand Ground Cinnamon because it could be contaminated with elevated levels of lead, according to a recall alert. According to the recall notice, lead exposure can impact nearly every bodily system, with effects depending on dosage, duration, and an individual’s age and weight. Low-level, short-term exposure may not produce immediate symptoms, and no illnesses have been reported to date. items.x: SMITH COUNTY, Miss. (WLBT) - A teenager has lost their life after a fire in Smith County. The incident happened in the Center Ridge community, on County Road 82. Taylorsville Fire Department, Sylvarena Fire Department, Smith County Emergency Management, and Smith County Sheriff’s Office responded to the scene. The incident remains under investigation. items.t: When ‘I’ll never put you in a home’ meets real-life caregiving
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Caregiving promises are sometimes made during emotional moments. When a loved one says, “I’ll never put you in a home,” or “You can always live with me,” the words may come from love, but health, safety, money and caregiver capacity can change over time. The Aging Untold experts explain why families may feel guilt or pressure later and what to say instead. Why promises can create pressure Families often make promises before they have talked through what caregiving could involve, Amy O’Rourke, an aging expert, said. “They haven’t looked at the reality and talked about the reality at first,” O’Rourke said. “You know, ‘I’ll take care of you.’ But if these certain things happen, we’re going to have to have another conversation.” She said the questions can be practical: Can we afford the care? items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Many people think the first sign of shingles is a bad rash, but it can start with intense pain in the body. ‘Intense amount of burning’ Gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck said she had shingles twice and it was tied to an autoimmune condition, and described the pain as burning. “It burned. It’s an infection in the nerve, essentially. It is nerve pain at the highest level,” Cradduck said. She compared it to a toothache. “You know how intense a toothache is. Now think about that in a pathway, in a nerve pathway in your body,” Cradduck said. Her pain was on her back and flank. “Not something I could see, not something I could reach, but just an intense amount of burning. And then it came around,” she said. items.t: Better than blood? Researcher says new discovery could help save lives
items.x: KANSAS CITY, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) — A doctor and research scientist at the University of Missouri-Kansas City said he has discovered a potential alternative to blood transfusions for people with severe blood loss. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. Blood transfusions are currently the best treatment to try to stop severe blood loss, also known as hemorrhagic shock. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. items.t: What to look for in a clinical trial and why older adults should be included
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Clinical trials can be a proactive way to explore new treatments, but studies show older adults are often left out of them, even though many conditions affect older adults more often. The Aging Untold experts hosts are discussing what to look for when choosing a study and how to decide whether to take part. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. items.x: SEMINARY, Miss. (WLBT) - The Seminary Bulldogs beat the Magee Trojans 35-7 on Thursday night to win the 3A Region 6 title, their first region championship since 2018. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Oregon Zoo treating Tula-Tu for virus that killed another baby elephant
items.x: PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - Veterinary teams at the Oregon Zoo have started intensive treatment for an Asian elephant calf, Tula-Tu, infected with elephant endotheliotropic herpesvirus, or EEHV. Staff noticed changes in the behavior and energy levels of the calf, Tula-Tu, on Oct. 24. Technicians found a low white blood cell count during routine in-house screening, prompting veterinarians to start antiviral medications immediately, the zoo said in a statement shared with FOX 12 on Friday. The Oregon Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at Oregon State University confirmed an elevated viral load of EEHV the following day, leading the care team to administer plasma transfusions. Another baby elephant housed at the Oregon Zoo, 6-year-old Lily, succumbed to the virus in 2018. But staff say there’s hope this time. “Early detection is critical,” said Dr. Carlos Sanchez, the zoo’s animal health director.

items.t: How to check water safety before a lake or river outing

items.t: Driver cited after 75-year-old woman hit, killed on Hwy 99E in Oak Grove
items.x: OAK GROVE, Ore. (KPTV) - An elderly woman died Thursday after she was hit by a driver in Oak Grove, according to Oregon State Police. The crash happened at about 8:42 a.m. on Highway 99E. OSP said a driver in a white Kia Soul was going northbound near Holly Avenue when they hit 75-year-old Janice Mae Gilliland who was trying to cross the highway in an unmarked crosswalk. Gilliland was taken to a local hospital where she later died. The driver of the Kia, a 76-year-old woman, was cited for failing to stop and remain stopped for a pedestrian, according to OSP. Traffic on Highway 99E was impacted for about an hour due to the crash investigation.

Doctor cites human history outdoors Mann spent two years traveling the world, practicing medicine in remote environments. Across his years in medicine, he has found that being outside is one of the most powerful treatments. items.t: Portland-area photographer indicted on sex abuse, stalking charges; deputies seek more victims
items.x: WASHINGTON COUNTY, Ore. (KPTV) - A 36-year-old man was indicted this week on sexual abuse and stalking charges, and Washington County deputies believe there may be more victims. Abraham Daniel Lopez, of Beaverton, was arrested on Oct. 20. A grand jury indicted him on Oct. 28 on three counts of second-degree sexual abuse and stalking. The investigation began on Oct. 18 when a woman claimed she was being stalked by Lopez for several months. The sheriff’s office said deputies also learned Lopez engaged in unwanted sexual contact with the woman multiple times. According to the sheriff’s office, Lopez has worked in the Portland area as a photographer and may have met women through his work. Detectives believe there may be more victims who have yet to come forward. Anyone with information about Lopez can contact the Investigations Division at 503-846-2500 and reference case number 50-26-14807.

items.t: Man convicted of killing wife in 2010 dies in Oregon prison
items.x: UMATILLA, Ore. (KPTV) - A man convicted of murdering his wife in 2010 died Thursday morning at a prison in Umatilla, according to the Oregon Department of Corrections. Namegabe Mushegero, who was serving a life sentence, died in the infirmary at Two Rivers Correctional Institution. He was 68. The DOC said state police have been notified and the medical examiner will determine the cause of death. His next of kin has been notified. Mushegero admitted to killing his wife, Nabintu Kalamba, in 2010 by beating her with a hammer inside their Washington County apartment in front of their children. He later pleaded guilty to murder and was sentenced to life in prison.

Simon said cameras in the couple’s car recorded the events. The couple is staying anonymous out of fear of retaliation. items.t: Record number of female candidates in 2026 midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century. This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. items.t: 2026 midterms set new record for political ad spending
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterms have set a new record for political advertising spending, becoming the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history. With Election Day less than a week away, an estimated $11.21 billion has been spent or reserved for political advertisements, according to the ad-tracking firm AdImpact. That’s slightly more than the $11.2 billion spent during the entire 2024 election cycle and roughly $2.3 billion more than the 2022 midterms. “It’s not just that a lot of money is being spent, it’s that it’s very expensive to advertise this late in the campaign,” said Todd Belt, a political management professor at George Washington University. Some of the biggest spending has taken place in traditionally “red” states, where increasingly competitive Senate races have attracted hundreds of millions of dollars. items.t: 71-year-old grandmother missing after going on walk more than 3 weeks ago, police say
items.x: (Gray News) - A 71-year-old New Jersey woman went for a walk more than three weeks ago and hasn’t been seen since. Belinda Prentice was last seen about 6 p.m. Oct. 5 near Bamburgh Court off New Brunswick Road and Willow Avenue in Franklin Township, a press release said. Her granddaughter, Sienna Benjamin, said Prentice had shown signs of cognitive decline in recent years, and the family was working to determine whether she had dementia and to obtain guardianship, People reported. Franklin Township police and the family are urging residents to check doorbell and security cameras for possible sightings. Anyone with information is asked to call the Franklin Township Police Department at 732-873-2300.

items.t: 79-year-old man killed after collision with fire truck
items.x: WICHITA, Kan. ( KWCH /Gray News) - A 79-year-old man was killed in a crash involving a fire truck. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. The crash caused the vehicles to hit another vehicle, a black Dodge Ram. The 79-year-old man died at the hospital. He was identified by police as James Mattson of Wichita. The driver of the Dodge Ram was not hurt, nor were the four firefighters inside the fire truck. The WPD Critical Accident Team will investigate the crash.

items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.x: AUDUBON, Iowa ( KCRG /Gray News) - A teen is dead after being thrown from a tractor in a crash with a semi-truck. Iowa State Patrol said it happened Sunday night on Highway 71, just south of Audubon. A crash report said a semi-truck hit the back of the trailer that the tractor was pulling. Tatum Christensen, 16, was ejected from the tractor. He died at the scene. The report said the semi-truck driver was flown to the hospital with serious injuries. items.t: Salem man sentenced for sharing child sexual abuse material after FBI investigates online network
items.x: PORTLAND Ore. (KPTV) - A 38-year-old Salem man was sentenced to eight years in prison on Thursday for sharing child sexual abuse material (CSAM), according to the U.S. Attorney’s Office - District of Oregon. Robert Andrew Arias pleaded guilty in August 2026 to receiving, distributing and possessing CSAM. This comes after an FBI investigation into online networks people use to trade the illegal material. In December 2023, federal investigators seized digital devices in which they found illicit content. Following Arias’ prison term, he will spend 10 years on probation and be required to register as a sex offender. The court also confiscated all digital devices from Arias that he used to accesses and share the material. “This sentence sends a clear message: if you exploit children, we will find you and you will go to federal prison,” the U.S. Attorney said.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73

His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.x: VANCOUVER, Wash. (KPTV) - A jury has found Travis Ward guilty in connection with the deadly 2024 shooting at the Vancouver Mall. On Thursday, jurors found 32-year-old Ward guilty of first-degree murder, first-degree assault, witness tampering, and second-degree unlawful possession of a firearm. items.t: US Army practices digging mass battlefield graves
items.x: (Gray News) - The United States Army is now practicing mass battlefield graves, a practice not done since the Korean War. The Army reported that soldiers in North Carolina completed a “test-of-concept” exercise for large-scale battlefield temporary interment. “This exercise allowed us to take a critical look at how we respect, honor, and systematically manage our fallen in a high-intensity conflict,” said Sgt. 1st Class Delbert Ruede, the senior fatality management NCO for the 3rd CSC, in the release. Each plot is made up of five trenches designed to hold 100 bodies. During the exercises, soldiers reevaluated Korean War-era practices in how to excavate and backfill the plots without damaging the structure or human remains. The exercises also provided an opportunity for military chaplains and religious affairs specialists to train for mass-casualty environments.

items.t: Detroit organization promotes urban farming amid food insecurity
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Affordability remains the main talking point ahead of the 2026 midterms, and food accessibility is one issue voters may consider when heading to the polls. It’s estimated around 53 million Americans live in what’s called a “food desert,” lower-income areas without easy access to supermarkets or grocery stores. Most of those people live in urban areas, where fast food and convenience shops replace healthy, nutritious foods as the most affordable option. Food insecurity is economic, but it also relates to community and health, with a higher risk of obesity, heart disease and cancer in areas with low access. In Michigan, organizations like the Detroit Black Community Food Sovereignty Network are advocating for urban farming and food sovereignty. He calls the treatment “better than blood.” When someone experiences severe trauma, such as a car crash or gunshot wound, they risk bleeding to death. items.t: How caregivers can keep dignity intact when conversations get tense
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Stress can turn into sharp words when you are a caregiver for someone you love. The Aging Untold experts are sharing advice on how to communicate in a way that keeps dignity intact, builds cooperation and helps caregivers reset when a conversation escalates. Step away before things escalate “Sam” Cradduck, a gerontologist, said the first move to make when it feels like a conversation is about to escalate is to leave the room. “You have to step away. You really do,” Cradduck said. “You’ve got to let yourself calm down.” Aging well coach Katherine Ambrose said caregivers can take that step by removing themselves or getting help. “If you’re fantasizing about escaping, or noticing the yellow flags like you’re starting to get hot, shaky, your jaw’s tense, that’s a good time to go, ‘OK, my nervous system is at its limit,’” Ambrose said. Before moving in with her mother, Cathie lived in Richmond, Virginia, and had a career in a technical field. items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The 2026 midterm elections are set to be historic. More women are on state and federal ballots this cycle, with a record number running for the House of Representatives, according to Kelly Dittmar of the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University. Women make up 50% of the population and are the most consistent voting bloc in American elections, even though women have only been able to legally cast a ballot for just over a century. This year, an increase in candidates nationwide has led more women to run for office, with a historic number of women having been nominated ahead of the Nov. 3 election. “We have a record number of women running for the House overall, a record number of Democratic women running. Police said Wichita Fire Department Engine 20 was driving with emergency lights and sirens activated when a black Honda CRV driven by the 79-year-old man entered an intersection the fire truck was crossing. items.t: You’ll get an extra hour of sleep (or partying) on Halloween night as daylight saving time ends
items.x: (Gray News) — After a long night of trick-or-treating or partying, be prepared to get an extra hour of sleep. Daylight saving time will end on Nov. 1 at 2 a.m., also known as “fall back.” The United States will be back on standard time with more daylight in the morning and less in the evening. Daylight saving time will start again on March 14, 2027, also known as “spring forward.” The federal government has been discussing doing away with daylight saving time altogether, meaning clocks would not need to be changed at any point during the year. However, Congress failed to act before next weekend’s time change.

items.t: Legendary college football coach June Jones dies at 73
items.x: HONOLULU ( KHNL /Gray News) - Former University of Hawaii head football coach June Jones has died at the age of 73, according to multiple sources Thursday. June Jones was the winningest coach in the modern era of Hawaii football with 76 victories in nine seasons from 1999 through 2007. He went to work at Southern Methodist University from 2008 until he resigned in 2014. Jones led Hawaii to six bowl games and coached three seasons with 10 or more wins, including an undefeated 12-0 regular season and a trip to the Allstate Sugar Bowl in 2007. His 1999 squad recorded the biggest turnaround in NCAA history with a 9-4 record and a share of the Western Athletic Conference title and earned him National Coach of the Year honors. items.x: (Gray News) - Almost 340,000 space heaters are under recall throughout the United States due to the risk of fire and burns. DREO space heaters model DR-HSH015 were placed under recall on Oct. 29, the Consumer Product Safety Commission reported. About 338,800 units were affected, with an additional 36,300 sold in Canada. They were sold directly through DREO and other sites like Best Buy and Home Depot between Sept. 2025 and Oct. 2026. According to the recall, the affected space heaters can overheat and catch fire. DREO said they received 17 reports of ignition, three resulting in property damage and one burning a person’s hand. Anyone with a recalled unit should stop using the space heater immediately and contact DREO for a free space heater to replace the faulty one. items.t: ‘Star Trek’ actor Patrick Stewart dead at 86
items.x: (AP) - Patrick Stewart , the classically trained actor who added Shakespearean gravitas to the “Star Trek” and “X-Men” franchises, has died. He was 86. Stewart died Wednesday in Los Angeles, following “a brief and poignant journey” with Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy Body Dementia, spokesperson Kelly Bush Novak said. Stewart’s diagnoses had not been previously disclosed. While best known as Professor Charles Xavier and Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the “X-Men” and “Star Trek: The Next Generation” series and films, respectively, Stewart spent more of his career onstage than in the X-Mansion or on the USS Enterprise. items.x: MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - When meteorologists talk about El Niño, you often hear warnings about shifting jet streams, wetter winters across the South, and unusual severe weather setups. But not all El Niños are created equal. items.x: COLLIERVILLE, Tenn. (WMC) - A 37-year-old man faces vehicular homicide and DUI charges following a fatal four-vehicle crash Wednesday evening on Highway 385, according to the Collierville Police Department. Investigators said Derek Kyle Johnson was driving near the Progress Road overpass around 5:15 p.m. when the collision occurred. Two people, including Johnson, were injured and taken to a hospital, where one victim later died from their injuries. Johnson is charged with vehicular homicide, DUI, reckless driving, driving on a suspended license, an open container violation, and a seat belt violation. His bond has been set at $250,000.
